notes:
I have gathered substantial material from several of the permitted sources. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Luke 18:23–43 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 23 — *“But when the ruler heard this, he became very sad, because he was extremely wealthy.”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- The man’s sorrow was proportionate to his wealth. His unwillingness to part with his riches showed he valued them more than treasure in heaven. He is the only person in the Gospels who came to Jesus and went away in a worse condition. (Constable, StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-23.html)
- Mark adds that the man went away with a “lowering” or “frowning” look (Mark 10:22). Luke records his emotional response — he became “very sorrowful.” He essentially said, “I can’t do that; I can’t make that sacrifice.” (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- The Cambridge Bible notes that St Mark says “his brow grew gloomy and cloudy at the command.” Dante called this “il gran rifiuto” — “the great refusal” (Inferno 10:27). Nothing forbids us hoping the words of Jesus, who “loved him,” later sank into his soul. (Cambridge Bible, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-23.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary cites the *Gospel of the Hebrews* (a very early document): “Then the rich man began to scratch his head, for that was not to his mind. And the Lord said to him, How then canst thou say, I have kept the Law; for it is written in the Law, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself; and, lo! many of thy brethren, children of Abraham, live in the gutter, and die of hunger, while thy table is loaded with good things, and nothing is sent out to them?” (Pulpit, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-23.htm)
- Matthew Henry notes: “Many that are loth to leave Christ, yet do leave him. After a long struggle between their convictions and their corruptions, their corruptions carry the day.” (Henry, StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-23.html)
- Luke alone uses the phrase “very rich” (πλούσιος σφόδρα), whereas Matthew and Mark say “he had great possessions.” (Expositor’s Greek Testament, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-23.htm)

---

### v. 24 — *“Seeing the man’s sadness, Jesus said, ‘How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Jesus did not change the demands of discipleship when the rich man walked away; instead He used the occasion to teach. Riches are a problem because they make us satisfied with this life instead of longing for the age to come. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Mark adds that Jesus “looked round about” — following the departing youth with His eye — before speaking to His disciples. Mark 10:24 adds the explanation: “How hard it is for them that *trust in riches*” — the difficulty lies in conquering this idolatrous trust. (Ellicott, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-24.htm)
- The better manuscripts give simply, “When Jesus saw him, He said…” (Ellicott, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-24.htm)
- The Cambridge Bible notes that the real point Jesus wished to teach was that “riches are always a temptation and a snare” (cf. 1 Timothy 6:9–10). It was almost a proverb among the ancients that “the very rich are not good.” (Cambridge Bible, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-24.htm)

**Denominational / Theological Differences:**

- **Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin writes that riches “do not, in their own nature, hinder us from following God; but, in consequence of the depravity of the human mind, it is scarcely possible for those who have a great abundance to avoid being intoxicated by them. So they who are exceedingly rich are held by Satan bound, as it were, in chains.” He interprets “camel” (v.25) as meaning a ship’s rope (κάμιλος), not the animal. (Calvin, CCEL — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol32/htm/lxxii.htm)

---

### v. 25 — *“Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- This is a proverbial expression denoting, literally, a thing impossible — but figuratively, very difficult. (JFB, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-25.htm)
- The Cambridge Bible systematically refutes attempts to soften the saying: (i) the conjecture “kamilon” (rope) for “kamelon” (camel) is “wholly without authority”; (ii) the “needle’s eye” as a small side-gate is probably a modern notion that originated from attempts to soften this verse — there is no ancient trace of it; (iii) Babylonian Talmudic parallels substitute “an elephant” for “a camel,” proving the literal animal is meant; (iv) the proverb’s object is to express human impossibility. (Cambridge Bible, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-25.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary adds that the simile was common among the Jews, the Talmud gives the parallel of an elephant through a needle’s eye, and the Koran repeats the very words. (Pulpit, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-25.htm)
- Luke alone uses βελόνη (belonē) for “needle” — the classical and surgical term — while Matthew and Mark use ῥαφίς (rhaphis), a word stigmatized by Greek grammarians as barbarous. This is a mark of Luke’s culture and medical background. (Vincent’s Word Studies, BibleHub — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-25.htm; also Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-25.htm)

**Catholic Reading:**

- Orchard’s Catholic Commentary says: “There is no need to suggest the usual far-fetched interpretations of ‘camel’ and ‘needle’s eye’ in order to tone down the severity of our Lord’s warning; the words mean what they say.” Riches in themselves are neither good nor bad; it is undue attachment that keeps men out of the Kingdom. God can save the rich by inspiring them to give wealth away or by enabling them to act as good stewards without renunciation (cf. the parable of 16:1–9). (Orchard, StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/luke-18.html)

---

### v. 26 — *“Those who heard this asked, ‘Who then can be saved?’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- The hearers’ response is true to human nature: we find it hard to see how riches can hinder us from the Kingdom. We think only of the blessing and good that riches might bring. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Matthew Henry notes the disciples do not find fault with what Christ required as hard or unreasonable. “They know how closely the hearts of most men cleave to this world, and are ready to despair of their being ever brought to this.” (Henry, StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-23.html)

---

### v. 27 — *“But Jesus said, ‘What is impossible with man is possible with God.’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Jesus confirms the disciples’ conclusion that salvation is humanly impossible — but adds that God Himself will save those who adopt the dispositions Jesus has recommended. (Orchard, StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/luke-18.html)
- Matthew Henry: “There are such difficulties in the way of our salvation as could never be got over but by pure omnipotence, by that grace of God which is almighty… His grace can work upon the soul, so as to alter the bent and bias of it, and give it a contrary ply.” (Henry, StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-23.html)
- Guzik: “Having and keeping the heart of a giver will keep you from being corrupted by riches.” (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)

---

### v. 28 — *“‘Look,’ said Peter, ‘we have left all we had to follow You.’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- In contrast to the rich young ruler, the disciples did give up everything (or most everything) to follow Jesus. Peter wondered what reward would be promised to them who obeyed where the rich young ruler disobeyed. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Matthew Henry: “There is an aptness in us to speak too much of what we have left and lost, of what we have done and suffered, for Christ. This appears in Peter… But this we should be so far from boasting of, that we should rather acknowledge it not worth taking notice of.” (Henry, StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-23.html)

---

### vv. 29–30 — *“Truly I tell you… no one who has left home or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God will fail to receive many times more in this age—and in the age to come, eternal life.”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- The twelve may have their unique reward, but there will be universal honour for all who sacrifice for Jesus’ sake. “Many times more” (or “manifold more”) is obviously not meant in a material sense — Jesus did not promise a hundred literal mothers or wives. It is literal but spiritual in its fulfilment. Matthew Poole described the returns as: joy in the Holy Ghost, peace of conscience, the sense of God’s love, contentment, and God stirring up others to supply wants. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- The principle stands: God will be a debtor to no man. It is impossible for us to give more to God than He gives back. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Mark adds the phrase “with persecutions” (Mark 10:30), tempering any triumphalism. (Calvin, CCEL — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol32/htm/lxxiii.htm)

**Debated Popular Teaching — Prosperity / Word of Faith:**

- Prosperity preachers commonly cite this passage (and Mark 10:29–30) to teach a “hundredfold return” on financial giving. They define the return as material wealth. However, as Guzik’s Q&A notes: “If that’s what Jesus meant, what do we do with His reference to the reward of a hundredfold? If you give a house, do you get a tract of houses back? … Such a crass, materialistic promise was not at all what Jesus had in mind.” The “hundredfold” refers to what one gains in the Kingdom of God — spiritual family and eternal blessings. (Guzik/Enduring Word Q&A — https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/is-prosperity-gospel-biblical-live-qa-with-pastor-lance-ralston-on-may-2-2024-2/)
- A Catholic apologetics article similarly notes that prosperity preachers misuse Mark 10:30 and Luke 6:38: “If we aren’t literally going to have hundreds of new family members in this life as a reward for leaving some, why should we believe that we’ll literally have hundreds of new possessions?” (Catholic Answers — https://shop.catholic.com/blog/does-jesus-promise-us-health-and-wealth/)
- Ligonier describes the prosperity teaching that “Jesus purchased complete physical healing for His people in this life” and that believers can “name it and claim it” through faith — a distortion of passages like this one. (Ligonier — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/field-guide-on-false-teaching-prosperity-gospel)

---

### v. 31 — *“Then Jesus took the Twelve aside and said to them, ‘Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled.’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- This is the third major passion prediction in the Synoptic Gospels (cf. Luke 9:23, 44; 12:50; 13:32–33; 17:25). Jesus takes the Twelve aside privately. From this point Luke resumes his parallel with the other Synoptics for the final journey to Jerusalem. (StudyLight.org, Pulpit excerpts — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-31.html)
- Constable notes: “Jesus’ passion announcements to His disciples constitute important structural markers in Mark’s Gospel. Luke and Matthew did not use them this way.” Luke presented this as part of his travelogue (Luke 9:51 to 19:27). (Constable, StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)
- Luke plays down the amazement and fear of the disciples that Mark stressed, and instead focuses attention on their failure to understand. (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)

---

### vv. 32–33 — *“He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon. They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again.”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Many prophets had spoken of the Lord’s suffering: Psalm 22:12–18, the Servant Songs of Isaiah (especially 52:13–53:12), and Zechariah 13:7. (StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-31.html)
- Constable notes this is Jesus’ first reference to the Gentiles’ role in His trial and death. “Luke’s inclusion of this detail suggests that he did not want his Gentile readers to miss the guilt of Gentiles for Jesus’ death.” (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)
- “Jesus never spoke of his death without speaking of his resurrection.” God would not allow His Holy One to see corruption (Psalm 16:8–11). (StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-31.html)

---

### v. 34 — *“But the disciples did not understand any of these things. The meaning was hidden from them, and they did not comprehend what He was saying.”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Luke alone repeats three times that the disciples failed to comprehend. He strongly suggests their failure was due to God withholding this understanding (cf. Luke 24:16, 25–26). The illumination of believers is a necessary, supernatural work of God’s Spirit. (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)
- Guzik adds that this spiritual blindness may have been merciful: “understanding too early might have caused them to abandon Him.” (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Constable: “The Twelve probably would not believe that such a fate would befall Jesus.” There is a continuation of the theme of responding to Jesus’ words: the rich ruler failed to respond to the good news; the disciples, though believing, failed to respond to the bad news. (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)

---

### v. 35 — *“As Jesus drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting beside the road, begging.”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Mark 10:46 gives the blind man’s name: Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Constable explains the apparent contradiction with Matthew (who says Jesus was leaving Jericho and mentions two blind men) and Mark (leaving Jericho, one blind man). The most widely accepted evangelical explanation: there were two Jerichos in Jesus’ day — the ancient city and the newer Roman city. The miracle happened between them, leaving one and entering the other. (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html; also Guzik — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Matthew mentions two blind men; Mark and Luke focus on the more prominent one, Bartimaeus. (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)

---

### vv. 36–37 — *“When he heard the crowd going by, he asked what was happening. ‘Jesus of Nazareth is passing by,’ they told him.”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- The blind man could not see Jesus, but he could hear Him. Instead of giving up because he could not seek Jesus by sight, he sought Jesus the way he could — by hearing. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)

---

### v. 38 — *“So he called out, ‘Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- “Son of David” was a messianic title expressing faith in Jesus as Israel’s promised Messiah (cf. Luke 1:27, 32; 2 Samuel 7:8–16; Isaiah 11:1, 10). Like the tax collector (v.13), he called for mercy without claiming any merit. (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)
- “The blind man knew he needed mercy from Jesus. He didn’t think that God owed him; he wanted mercy.” (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)

---

### v. 39 — *“Those who led the way admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, ‘Son of David, have mercy on me!’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- The man was desperate to get Jesus’ attention. He would not be embarrassed, and he would not be shut up. Opposition only made him more adamant. His insistence reflected his belief that Jesus could help him and his hope that Jesus would help him. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/; Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)

---

### vv. 40–41 — *“Jesus stopped and directed that the man be brought to Him. When he had been brought near, Jesus asked him, ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’ ‘Lord,’ he said, ‘let me see again.’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Nothing could stop Jesus on His journey to Jerusalem, yet He stood still to answer a persistent plea for mercy. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Jesus asked the question to elicit the blind man’s faith. He certainly knew what the man wanted. The title “Lord” here reflects more than simple respect; it expressed the man’s faith. (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)
- The blind man knew how to submit to Jesus: he called Jesus “Lord” and simply asked. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)

---

### v. 42 — *“‘Receive your sight!’ Jesus replied. ‘Your faith has healed you.’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- Jesus connected the man’s healing with the man’s faith. Jesus’ words left no doubt that He was responsible for the miracle, yet He clarified that the man’s faith was the instrumental cause — divine power was the efficient cause. Luke stresses this pattern repeatedly (cf. Luke 7:50; 8:48; 17:19). (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)
- The Greek verb translated “has healed you” (σέσωκέν, *sesōken*) is the same word for “saved.” The man received both physical sight and spiritual salvation. (Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)

---

### v. 43 — *“Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus, glorifying God. And all the people who saw this gave praise to God.”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- The healing was instantaneous. The man began following Jesus — the way of Jesus became his way — and he glorified God. Only Luke records the glorifying and praising of God that took place, reflecting his characteristic interest in the joyful outcome of salvation (cf. Luke 2:20; 5:25–26; Acts 2:47; 3:9). (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html; Guzik/Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Luke probably included this incident to contrast the faith of the blind man with the unbelief of the religious leaders, and (by extension) with the rich ruler who walked away sorrowful. The humble outcast — like the tax collector earlier in the chapter — received salvation and healing through faith, while the rich ruler who failed to realize his need went away empty. (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-18.html)

---

### Summary of Distinctive Interpretations

**Reformed (Calvin):** On v.25, Calvin understood “camel” (κάμηλος) as a sailor’s rope (κάμιλος), softening the hyperbole somewhat. He emphasized that riches are not inherently evil but that human depravity makes it “scarcely possible” for the wealthy to avoid intoxication by them. On vv.29–30, he notes the promise includes “persecutions” (Mark 10:30), guarding against a triumphalist reading. (CCEL — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol32/htm/lxxii.htm; https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol32/htm/lxxiii.htm)

**Catholic:** Orchard’s commentary stresses that the camel/needle saying means exactly what it says — no need to soften it. Riches are not intrinsically bad; it is *undue attachment* that bars one from the Kingdom. God can save the rich either by moving them to renunciation or by enabling faithful stewardship. (StudyLight.org — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/boc/luke-18.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises that Jesus’ command to sell everything was a *specific* word for a *specific* man — not a universal command. Many rich people can do more good by continuing to make money and using it for God’s glory. The blind man’s persistence despite opposition is held up as the model of the faith Jesus looks for. On the “hundredfold” reward, Guzik explicitly rejects the prosperity gospel’s materialistic reading. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)

**Prosperity / Word of Faith (critiqued by multiple sources):** Prosperity preachers cite vv.29–30 (and Mark 10:30) to teach a literal “hundredfold” financial return on giving. Guzik, Ligonier, and Catholic Answers all refute this: the “manifold more” Jesus promised is spiritual — family in the Kingdom of God, joy, peace, and eternal life — not a guaranteed monetary multiplication. (https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/is-prosperity-gospel-biblical-live-qa-with-pastor-lance-ralston-on-may-2-2024-2/; https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/field-guide-on-false-teaching-prosperity-gospel; https://shop.catholic.com/blog/does-jesus-promise-us-health-and-wealth/)

**Modern Scholarship / Text-Critical Note (v.25):** BibleHub’s text-critical summary confirms that all early majuscule manuscripts read κάμηλον (“camel”). The variant κάμιλον (“thick rope” or “ship’s cable”) is late and geographically isolated. The canonical reading is secure. (https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Luke_18_25_s_camel_metaphor.htm)
